/.reason: Two numbers I can verify in a reference check, then the scope in one clause; that is how I read a qualifications package.

/design-build/.reason: A builder who has to run the plant afterward has skin in the design choices; that is the design-build incentive I actually want to see, and 'on the hook' does not say how.

/design-build/modular-data-centers/.reason: Interfaces are where every modular program I have reviewed either worked or did not; a vendor who leads with that has read the same failure reports I have.

/design-build/hyperscale-data-centers/.reason: Sizing shared infrastructure for phase one without stranding phases two through four is the actual campus design problem; A names it, C just describes my inbox.

/design-build/ai-data-centers/.reason: Power, cooling and structure as one basis of design before the GPU PO lands is the sequencing I fight for on every AI program; A says it in one line, B only says it hurts.

/design-build/planning-feasibility/.reason: Energization is the gate that kills sites, and calling feasibility a decision list instead of a deliverable is how I would write the scope myself.

/design-build/design-engineering/.reason: 'Operating requirements' is the OPR I write; a design team that promises to carry it through without a field re-engineering cycle is speaking to my document, not their brochure.

/design-build/preconstruction-procuremen.reason: Long-lead gear, scope gaps and field constraints are the three columns of my preconstruction risk register; A lists them, B overclaims with 'every'.

/design-build/data-center-construction/.reason: A GC whose job ends at integrated systems testing rather than substantial completion is the one I shortlist; the safety number in A is impressive but I would need to see how 'recorded' is defined.

/design-build/commissioning-turnover/.reason: Acceptance is my signature, and B frames commissioning as the burden of proof before that signature rather than a deliverable; that is the right side of the table to be on.

/design-build/expansions-retrofits/.reason: 'Operating constraint first' is the MOP mindset; A promises no risk to running systems, which nobody doing live-environment work should promise.

/power-generation/.reason: 5.3 GW is a number I can check, and 'after the utility says no' is the interconnection queue problem every one of my clients is living in right now.

/power-generation/backup-power-systems/.reason: Every backup failure I have investigated was in paralleling controls, ATS logic or fuel, never the engine block; B knows where the system actually lives.

/maintenance/.reason: Three named service lines beat two sentences of reassurance; I need to know whether 'maintenance' includes monitoring and support, and C answers that.

/maintenance/preventive-maintenance/.reason: Template PM programs are how a facility ends up doing quarterly IR scans on gear that needs monthly and annual on gear that needs none; C names the actual defect in most PM contracts.

/data-center-markets/.reason: Lists the five markets so I can find mine in one glance, and admits the decisions differ by type instead of pretending one template fits all.

/data-center-markets/colocation/.reason: Names the three actual scopes, halls, power upgrades and retrofits, inside a live facility; A promises zero interruption, which is not a promise a competent contractor makes.

/data-center-markets/enterprise/.reason: 'Power conversions' is a scope line I can put in an RFP; the other two are attitude.

/insights/.reason: Guidance from people who then have to build to it is the only kind I forward to clients; C names my calendar but does not say what it is.

/about/.reason: Founding year, project count, gigawatts, single specialty: that is the first paragraph of the qualifications section I ask for, and it is all here.

/about/leadership/.reason: Thirteen is a number, and a leadership page is where I check whether the bench is deep enough to staff my program; C says come count.

/contact/.reason: A contact page needs to tell me the form goes to someone who can act, not to a CRM; C says so, B is just a label.

/support/.reason: Routing to someone who already knows the facility is the whole value of a support page; A says it, the others are signage.

/start-a-project/.reason: 'Fit' means they are willing to say it is not their project, which is the one thing I want from an intake form before I spend a client's time.

/request-service/.reason: Facility and system are the two fields a dispatcher actually needs, and 'today' is a response commitment I would hold them to; B's 'discussion' is the wrong word when something is down.

/thank-you/.reason: After I submit something I want the timeline and who calls; A promises that and nothing else.

/sitemap/.reason: A sitemap is a utility page; label it as one and get out of the way.

/solutions/.reason: Six program types named in the H1 means I can find AI and modular without scrolling; that is what a hub page is for.

/solutions/ai-hpc-data-centers/.reason: Designing for the GPU you have and the one after it is the density-trajectory problem, rack kW, liquid loop, MV distribution, and B is the only headline that admits the second generation exists.

/solutions/edge-data-centers/.reason: A repeatable edge program is a reference design plus a shop plus logistics; A names all three, B is the same sentence with the engineering removed.

/solutions/modular-data-centers/.reason: Site, power and commissioning plan are the three interface documents I make modular vendors sign up to; B lists them and names the shop I can go audit.

/solutions/colocation-data-centers/.reason: The SLA is the constraint that actually governs live colo work, it defines the windows and the concurrent maintainability you have to preserve, and C is the only one that names it.

/solutions/greenfield-new-builds/.reason: Six named phases is a scope of services I can map directly to the RFP sections; 'a hundred decisions' is a nice line I cannot evaluate.

/solutions/brownfield-retrofit/.reason: Three scopes, live environment, operating constraint: that is the MOP-driven framing I need, and it does not promise the impossible zero-risk cutover.

/insights/data-center-site-selection-pow.reason: Energization is the binary outcome all the site decisions collapse to, interconnect queue, substation capacity, gas, water, and C makes the article about that outcome.

/insights/modular-vs-traditional-data-ce.reason: 'Compare the interfaces, not the labels' is the sentence I have been trying to get proposal evaluators to internalize for years; B is the equally legitimate second question.

/insights/ai-data-center-infrastructure-.reason: The GPU PO is the milestone my clients anchor everything to, so a checklist keyed to that date is one I would actually open in a kickoff.

/insights/hyperscale-campus-phasing/.reason: Phase one sabotaging phase four is exactly how it happens, a substation sized for phase one, a chilled-water header with no future tap, and the how-to framing promises a method, not a manifesto.

/insights/data-center-commissioning-chec.reason: Acceptance is the owner's decision and 'proven' puts the burden where it belongs; I will read it to see whether their proof list matches my Level 5 IST script.

/insights/data-center-preventive-mainten.reason: A completed task list is what I get from most PM vendors and it tells me nothing about remaining life or trend; B names the problem I keep writing into O&M scopes.

/insights/data-center-monitoring-vs-dcim.reason: I have watched clients buy DCIM licenses for a facility that only needed BMS alarm routing; 'before you buy the dashboard' is the correct warning.

/insights/responsible-data-center-develo.reason: Power, water, noise and land are the four line items in every opposition packet; a piece organized around them is one I can hand to the entitlements consultant.
